title: Area VIII review: Fundamentals of Flight
intro: These questions mix the four Tasks of Area VIII: straight-and-level flight, level turns, climbs and climbing turns, and descents and descending turns. Many join two of them in one first-lessons instructing situation, such as a level-off and retrim after a climb or the rollout from a gliding turn, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: Before a new learner's first lessons on straight-and-level flight and then climbs, you plan to put removable tape reference lines on the windshield, because she keeps losing the nose picture. How does the AFH say to set them up?
options: One horizontal line marked on the ramp with the airplane level; because the horizon reference point is the same at any altitude, that single line also serves for cruise, slow flight and the climb picture later on

Vertical lines on the ground, airplane on a marked centerline and her seated normally; several horizontal lines in flight, as cruise and slow flight need different pitch attitudes. Remove them once she knows where to look

All lines marked from the right seat during your demonstration, so she copies your sight picture exactly; matching the instructor's picture is how the AFH says beginners learn where the nose belongs on the horizon

All lines marked in flight during the first lesson, vertical and horizontal alike, and left in place until the private pilot practical test so she never has to relearn where the nose and both wingtips belong on the horizon
questions.why: The AFH says reference points depend on the pilot's seating position, height and posture, so they start on the ground with the seat set normally. Vertical lines are best set on the ground with the airplane on a marked centerline and the learner seated properly; horizontal lines are best set in flight, such as in slow flight and cruise, and there are several because pitch attitudes vary. These aids are needed only for a short period [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. A single ramp line misses that: the horizon point is the same at any altitude, but the pitch attitudes are not. Your right-seat picture is not hers, since a side-by-side pilot sits off the longitudinal axis [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

questions.q: Climbing at 750 fpm to 4,500 feet, your learner starts the level-off at 4,425 feet and keeps climb power, as you briefed. Now level at 4,500, the airspeed builds toward cruise. What must she do with pitch while it builds?
options: Hold the first level attitude fixed until cruise speed; with the wings level, a change in airspeed does not change lift, so any pitch change now would only start a descent
Raise the nose slightly as the speed builds, so the airspeed does not overshoot cruise before she reduces the power to the cruise setting and retrims
Nothing yet: she should first reduce to cruise power, because climb power at a level attitude overspeeds the engine, then fix pitch
Lower the nose gradually, in step with the acceleration: as speed and lift grow, the angle of attack has to come down or the airplane climbs. At cruise speed, set cruise power and retrim
questions.why: The level-off lead is 10 percent of the climb rate: 0.10 x 750 = 75 feet, so 4,500 - 75 = 4,425 feet. The AFH then has climb power kept temporarily so the airplane accelerates, and at cruise speed the power is set to cruise and the airplane retrimmed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. While it accelerates, lift rises with speed, so the angle of attack must be decreased, timed with the speed change; too slowly and the airplane climbs, too fast and it descends [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]]. The IFH says the same: constant pitch changes are needed as the airspeed increases [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Pulling power at once is wrong: the AFH keeps climb power so the airplane reaches cruise speed.

questions.q: On lesson four your learner flies straight-and-level and level turns well, so you add AIH distractions. You plan to drop a pencil and ask her to pick it up. When does it fit best?
options: In straight-and-level flight, not partway through a turn: a head movement in a different plane during a prolonged turn can set off the Coriolis illusion. Even then, have her pick it up with minimal head movement

In the middle of a prolonged 30° level turn, because the AIH says the most effective distraction training is the hardest one, and turns are where most inadvertent stalls happen in normal flying, so that is where to test her
Only on the ramp before engine start, because the AIH says any distraction during flight practice takes too much of a beginner's attention from flying the airplane
Right as she starts the rollout from a long level turn, because the leans develop only in straight flight and the head movement helps reset her balance sense
questions.why: Drop a pencil is on the AIH list of distractions, and the AIH calls creating distractions while the learner practices maneuvers the most effective training, with the instructor teaching how to divide attention [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. The PHAK warns that after a turn has lasted long enough, a head movement in a different plane can create the Coriolis illusion, and says to retrieve dropped objects with minimal head movement [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. So give it in straight flight. The ramp-only option is wrong because the AIH wants these distractions in flight.

questions.q: In cruise at constant power in a fixed-pitch trainer, your learner looks down at a chart. You hear the wind noise rising and the engine note climbing. What is most likely happening, and what do you teach?
options: The nose has risen: a rising engine note in a fixed-pitch airplane means the pitch attitude is increasing, so she should lower the nose a little against the horizon and then check the altimeter
The power has crept up by itself; she should ease the throttle back until the engine note sounds normal again and leave the pitch attitude where it is
The nose has dropped: rising air noise likely means more speed and less pitch, and a fixed-pitch engine sounds higher as pitch decreases. Teach her to react: look out and reset the nose
Nothing she needs to act on yet: a change in sound in level flight means little, so she should wait until the altimeter or VSI confirms a trend
questions.why: The AFH says rising rushing-air noise likely means airspeed increasing and pitch decreasing, and in a fixed-pitch airplane the engine sound increases as pitch decreases; the instructor teaches perceiving and reacting to these cues, not just noticing them [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]. With power constant, airspeed stays essentially constant in straight-and-level, so a speed change points to pitch, which is corrected against the natural horizon and then cross-checked [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. The same sound cue is one of the three airspeed references in glides [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Waiting for the altimeter is the habit to break, not teach.

questions.q: Your learner flies a 15-minute straight-and-level leg to the practice area, where you will begin level turns. On the way she holds heading well but never moves her head from straight ahead. Which plan fits the sources?
options: Keep the scan yourself during the transit so she can concentrate on heading and altitude, then hand her the lookout duties at the practice area before the first clearing turn, since she has enough to do on the leg
Let her keep looking straight ahead in straight-and-level flight, since traffic on a collision course always shows up ahead of the nose; scanning to the sides belongs to turns
Have her watch the ADS-B In display instead of scanning outside on the transit leg, since it shows every nearby aircraft and keeps her head still for straight-and-level
Have her clear at periodic intervals on the long straight leg and make clearing turns before the first practice turn, calling 'clear left, right, above, and below.' The scan is hers too
questions.why: The PHAK says that during sustained straight-and-level flight a pilot should clear at periodic intervals, and in training make clearing turns before a practice maneuver with the learner calling out 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Learners who think the instructor handles the scan never build the habit, and instructors were aboard in 37 percent of the midair collisions in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. ADS-B In helps, but not every aircraft shows on it, and the AIM says to scan the whole sky rather than focus straight ahead [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

questions.q: You want your learner to fly a standard-rate level turn at 110 knots true airspeed. Using the PHAK rate-of-turn formula, about what bank does it take, and which instrument confirms the rate?
options: About 17°; the turn coordinator, whose second mark shows a standard-rate turn of 3° per second
About 17°; the attitude indicator, whose second bank mark shows standard rate at any airspeed
About 30°; the turn coordinator, whose miniature wing on the second mark shows 30° of bank
About 11°; the turn coordinator, because a faster airplane needs less bank for the same rate of turn
questions.why: Rate of turn equals 1,091 times the tangent of the bank divided by true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. For 3° per second: tan(bank) = 3 x 110 / 1,091 = 0.302, so the bank is about 16.8°, about 17°. The PHAK adds that a higher airspeed needs more bank for the same rate, not less [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. The turn coordinator's second mark shows a standard-rate turn, 3° per second, and it shows only rate and direction of turn, not bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. Set the bank on the cowling and horizon first, then confirm inside [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

questions.q: During your right-seat demonstration of level turns, you describe where the nose sits on the horizon. Your learner in the left seat says her picture does not match yours, and it differs between left and right turns. What do you teach?
options: Her picture should match yours once she stops leaning away from the turn, because parallax is the same from either seat; correct her posture first and the two pictures will line up in both directions
References depend on seat position, and she sits left of the roll axis: the nose seems to rise in her left turns and drop in her right turns. Build her picture from her seat for each direction
Left and right turns should look the same from any seat, so a difference between them means she is not coordinating the rudder; have her check the ball and center it first
Have her ignore the nose in turns and fly them by the attitude indicator until her pictures match yours, since the instrument looks the same from either seat in the airplane
questions.why: The AFH says reference points depend on the pilot's seating position, height and posture [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. With side-by-side seats the pilot sits off the longitudinal axis, typically to the left, so parallax makes the nose appear to rise in a left turn and descend in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Your seat is on the other side, so your picture is not hers; the sources do not describe the right-seat view, which is why you build hers from the left seat. Leaning away from the turn is a separate error to fix [[24:76|AFH 3-15]], and turning solely by instrument reference is a listed level turn error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

questions.q: In a low-wing trainer, your learner is in a straight climb and about to roll into a right climbing turn toward the practice area. Per the AIM, which clearing technique fits this airplane before the turn?
options: Momentarily raise the right wing and look, since in a low-wing airplane the wing hides the airspace above the turn; then roll in and hold the bank steady
No new clearing is needed if she cleared before the climb began, since the AIM asks for clearing turns only before stalls, spins and other advanced maneuvers
Momentarily lower the right wing and look, call 'clear right' out loud, then roll in; in the climb, keep making gentle banks to see the sky the nose hides
Raise the nose a little higher before the turn so she can see over the cowling, then roll in at once, because a low wing already gives a clear view into the turn
questions.why: The AIM says that in a low-wing airplane the pilot momentarily lowers the wing in the direction of the intended turn and looks; raising it is the high-wing technique. It also says clearing should precede all turns, including climbs and straight-and-level [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. The PHAK asks for gentle banks left and right during climbs and descents for continuous scanning, and for the learner to call 'clear left, right, above, and below' during instruction [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. The climb attitude itself creates blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]], so raising the nose further hides more.

questions.q: Your learner is in a 20° gliding right turn at best glide, turning from 120 to 210. Where should she start the rollout, and which control change avoids the most common problem when returning to a straight glide?
options: At about 200, leading by half the bank; and release the extra back pressure held in the turn, or the nose pitches up and the glide speed decays
At about 190, leading by the full bank angle; and add back pressure as the wings come level so the nose does not drop below the normal glide picture
At about 210, since a gliding turn stops as soon as the ailerons are neutral; then add a little power to bring the glide speed back to best glide
At about 200, leading by half the bank; and hold firm right rudder all through the rollout, since rudder pressures are higher with the power off
questions.why: The turn from 120 to 210 is 90° to the right. The AFH rule of thumb leads the rollout by half the bank: half of 20° is 10°, so start at 200 [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Returning from a gliding turn to a normal glide, the back pressure applied in the turn must be decreased or the airplane may pitch up and lose airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Firm rudder is the tempting wrong answer: with the power off, rudder pedal pressures are reduced, and excessive rudder during recovery from gliding turns is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

questions.q: Your learner's coordination in cruise level turns is good. In a right climbing turn at VY, the ball goes off center on every roll-in even though she uses the same rudder she uses in cruise turns. What do you explain?
options: Adverse yaw is the same at every airspeed, so her rudder is right; the ball moves because the bank is too steep for a climbing turn and should be kept under 10°
Rolling right, P-factor cancels most of the adverse yaw, so she is holding too much right rudder from cruise habit and should relax it during the roll-in
In climbing turns the propeller effects coordinate the airplane by themselves, so she should take her feet off the pedals and let the ball settle on its own

At low airspeed and high angle of attack, the rudder needed to cancel adverse yaw is greatest, and rolling right at low speed and high power, adverse yaw adds to the left yaw of P-factor. She needs much more right rudder than in cruise
questions.why: The PHAK says the rudder needed to counter adverse yaw is greatest at low airspeeds, high angles of attack and large aileron deflections [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]. The AFH explains that rolling right at low airspeed and high power, left adverse yaw adds to the left-yawing P-factor, so substantial right rudder is needed; rolling left, P-factor cancels some adverse yaw and less right rudder is needed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. That second case is the tempting wrong answer. All the factors of level turns, including adverse yaw and propeller effects, apply in climbing turns [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

questions.q: Your learner will level off at 3,000 feet and stay at the climb airspeed to start the next exercise, instead of accelerating to cruise. Which level-off technique matches the IFH?
options: Lower the nose to the level attitude for that airspeed and reduce power at the same time, in step with the pitch change, so the airspeed stays constant
Keep climb power after leveling until the airspeed settles, then reduce power to the cruise setting and retrim for straight-and-level flight at the new altitude
Reduce power first and hold the climb attitude until the vertical speed reads zero, then lower the nose to the level picture
Lower the nose briskly right at 3,000 feet with no lead, since the airplane stops climbing as soon as the nose comes down
questions.why: The IFH says that to level off at climbing airspeed, lower the nose to the pitch attitude for that airspeed in level flight while reducing power to the setting for that airspeed; if the power comes off in proportion to the pitch change, airspeed stays constant. It also uses a lead of about 10 percent of the vertical speed, because the airplane keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Keeping climb power is the AFH technique for leveling at cruise speed, so the airplane would accelerate past climb speed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

questions.q: Starting a climb from straight-and-level cruise, your learner raises the nose to the climb picture but forgets to add power. The VSI shows a good climb at first, then the rate falls off while the airspeed keeps dropping. What do you explain?
options: The wing makes less lift once the path tilts upward, so she needs more back pressure to keep the same rate; power only matters for climbs steeper than 10°
The power needed to hold an airspeed is the same in a climb as in level flight, so the airspeed will come back to cruise speed by itself if she waits

In level cruise thrust only equals drag. Raising the nose without power trades airspeed for altitude, and on an upward path part of the weight acts rearward, so the speed bleeds off. A sustained climb needs excess power, added with the pitch change
The climb rate fell only because she let the nose sag; climb performance is the same with or without added power as long as the pitch is held
questions.why: In steady level flight thrust equals drag [[1:262|PHAK 11-6]]. The PHAK names two ways to climb: with excess power above that needed for level flight, or by converting airspeed to altitude, a zoom climb in which the airspeed keeps decreasing [[1:262|PHAK 11-6]] [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]. In a climb part of the weight acts rearward with drag, so with no added power the airspeed diminishes; once the path is stable, angle of attack and lift go back to about their level values, so the wing is not making less lift [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. The AFH has climb power added at the same time as the pitch change [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

questions.q: You are checking out a commercial learner in a trainer with a controllable-pitch propeller and cowl flaps. From cruise, which climb entry matches the AFH?
options: Throttle up first and the propeller control after it, so the engine never runs at high RPM with low manifold pressure; then close the cowl flaps to cut drag and hold right rudder for P-factor
Propeller control forward first, then climb power as the nose comes up; set cowl flaps to keep cylinder head temperatures in limits, with right rudder for P-factor and torque
Raise the nose and let the airspeed settle at VY before adding any power, so the propeller governor is not overloaded, and leave the cowl flaps where they were for cruise
Leave the propeller control at the cruise setting and add only throttle, since the propeller control is moved only for takeoff and landing; right rudder as needed
questions.why: The AFH has the straight climb entered by raising the nose to the climb attitude while simultaneously adding climb power; with an independently controllable-pitch propeller, the propeller control is advanced before the engine power is increased. Cowl flaps, if installed, are set to keep cylinder head temperatures within the manufacturer's specifications, and torque and P-factor are countered with right rudder and aileron pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Throttle first is the tempting wrong answer, but it reverses the AFH order, and closing the cowl flaps works against engine cooling in the climb.

questions.q: Your learner holds VY all the way from takeoff to 3,500 feet on every lesson. Once she is clear of obstacles, why do the sources suggest changing to a normal (cruise) climb?
options: A cruise climb gives the most altitude in the least time, so once the airplane is airborne it always beats VY for reaching the cruising altitude
A cruise climb is flown slower than VY, which gives her more time to react to a power failure and more altitude per mile over the ground
A cruise climb is required by regulation above 1,000 feet AGL near a nontowered airport, so that departing traffic stays at a predictable speed
Its higher airspeed gives better engine cooling, more control authority and a better view over the nose for traffic, and VY needs a much quicker response to a power failure to avoid a stall
questions.why: The AFH says the normal or cruise climb speed is generally higher than VY and gives better engine cooling, greater control authority and better visibility over the nose; VY gives the most altitude in a given time and is used when departing a runway without obstructions until it is safe to change to a cruise climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. It also says to consider a lower pitch cruise climb because VY needs a much quicker pilot response to a powerplant failure to prevent a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. The aircraft's attitude creates extra blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]], so the better view matters.

questions.q: In the 'learner tells, instructor does' step of the climbs lesson, you fly a VY climb while your learner talks you through it. She says, 'If the airspeed drops below VY, I will add power.' What does this show, and what do you do?
options: A sound plan: in a climb, power controls airspeed, so she should adjust the throttle and hold the pitch picture fixed; you only need to fix her callout of the climb power setting
Nothing yet: you cannot judge her understanding until she flies the climb herself, so let her try it and correct the airspeed control after the first attempt
A misconception caught early: power stays fixed at climb power and airspeed is controlled with elevator. Have her set the attitude on the horizon, then check the airspeed
A motor-skill gap, not a misconception: she understands the climb but needs more hand-flying practice to hold VY, so have her fly several climbs in a row
questions.why: The AIH says that in the learner tells, instructor does step, the learner organizes the steps and techniques while freed from flying, and the instructor can evaluate the learner's understanding [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Here the belief shows up before she is busy flying. The AFH says power is fixed at the climb power setting and airspeed is controlled with elevator pressure, with the pitch checked against the natural horizon and cross-checked on the instruments [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Setting climb pitch by the airspeed indicator and chasing it is the first AFH climb error [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

questions.q: From straight-and-level cruise, your learner wants to descend 1,000 feet at the same cruise airspeed. She lowers the nose and leaves the power where it was, and the airspeed rises well above cruise. What does she need to learn?
options: Lowering the nose alone always holds the cruise speed, so the extra speed means the airplane is out of trim; she should roll in nose-down trim until the airspeed comes back to cruise
In a descent part of the weight acts forward along the path, so to hold cruise speed the power must come back as the descent starts; then pitch down just enough to hold that speed
Hold the cruise pitch attitude and reduce power only, because in a constant-airspeed descent the pitch attitude must stay exactly where it was in level cruise flight
Leave the power in and accept the extra speed, which costs nothing in a descent and gets the airplane down to the lower altitude sooner than a power reduction
questions.why: The PHAK says that to descend at the same airspeed as in straight-and-level flight, the power must be reduced as the descent is entered, because a component of weight acts forward along the flight path [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. The AFH says a power reduction is needed to balance the forces if airspeed is to be maintained [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], and its energy rule is to reduce throttle so thrust is less than drag, then pitch down just enough to hold the desired speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Holding the cruise attitude with only a power cut is the tempting wrong answer: the AFH has the pitch lowered to keep the speed.

questions.q: Your learner flies good level turns, holding just the back pressure that keeps altitude. In her first 20° gliding turn she uses that same back pressure, and the airspeed creeps above best glide with the nose low. What do you explain?
options: A gliding turn needs less back pressure than a level turn, because with no propeller slipstream the airplane tends to pitch up; she should relax some pressure and let the speed settle back at best glide
She should add a little power in every gliding turn, because no airplane can hold its glide speed in a bank without some thrust to replace the lift used for turning
She should steepen the bank to about 30°, where the airplane holds its bank with neutral controls, so the nose stops dropping and the speed goes back to best glide
A gliding turn needs more back pressure than a straight glide or a level turn: lift is tilted, light pressures invite too much rudder, and the airplane tends to nose down with the power off
questions.why: The AFH lists three elements that push the nose down and increase glide speed in a gliding turn: less vertical lift because the lift is tilted, excessive rudder from the reduced control pressures, and the airplane's normal tendency to nose down with the power off. They make it necessary to use more back pressure than in a straight glide or a level turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The instructor should explain why coordination is harder in gliding turns [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Steepening to a medium bank changes only the aileron needed to hold the bank, not the pitch [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

questions.q: In one lesson your learner levels off from a 500 fpm climb and later from a 500 fpm practice glide, ending at cruise speed both times. What leads does the AFH give, and why do they differ?
options: About 50 feet for the climb, keeping climb power to accelerate after leveling; about 100 feet for the glide, adding cruise power at the lead point, since the lead depends on descent rate and the airspeed wanted at the end
50 feet for both, since the 10 percent rule depends only on the vertical speed shown, and the airspeed wanted at the end makes no difference
About 100 feet for the climb, because the airplane accelerates slowly at climb power, and 50 feet for the glide, because power stops a descent at once
No lead for either one: level at the target altitude and then set the power, because the 10 percent rule applies only when flying by instruments
questions.why: For climbs the AFH starts the level-off at about 10 percent of the climb rate, 50 feet at 500 fpm, and keeps climb power temporarily so the airplane accelerates to cruise [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. For a practice glide, the lead depends on the rate of descent and the desired airspeed at the end of the level-off: at 500 fpm with a final speed above glide speed, start about 100 feet above the target and add cruise power at the lead point [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The 10 percent rule is not an instruments-only rule: the AFH gives it for these visual maneuvers, and the IFH uses the same lead [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

questions.q: After slow flight practice, your learner sets up best glide toward a field for a simulated engine failure but leaves 10° of flaps down. She holds best glide speed exactly. What does the AFH say about her glide?
options: Flaps make no difference as long as she holds the best glide speed, because the glide ratio depends only on the airspeed flown and not on the configuration
The flaps add lift, so the glide path flattens and she reaches farther than she would with the flaps up; she should leave them down until the field is made, then use full flaps
The added drag needs a lower pitch to hold the speed, so the glide path steepens and the distance shrinks; to glide farthest, retract the drag devices if possible
She should keep the flaps and raise the nose a little below best glide speed to make up for the extra drag, so the glide stretches back to the planned distance
questions.why: The AFH says the highest glide ratio occurs at maximum L/D, so drag-producing items such as flaps, landing gear and cowl flaps matter: more drag needs a lower pitch attitude to hold the airspeed, which steepens the glide path and cuts the distance, so all drag-producing components should be eliminated if possible [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Slowing below best glide to stretch it breaks the AFH cardinal rule and can lead to landing short or a stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

questions.q: Your learner has learned to hold right rudder in climbs. In her first straight glide she keeps a little right pressure on, and the ball is off center. Why does the rudder need change from climb to glide?
options: Left-turning tendencies grow as the power comes off and the airspeed falls, so a glide needs even more right rudder than the climb did; she should press harder on the right pedal to center it
The design compensation for P-factor and slipstream is set for powered flight. In a glide those effects go away but the compensation stays, so slight left rudder is likely needed
No rudder is ever needed in a straight glide, because with the power off nothing yaws the airplane; the ball is off center only from light turbulence
The ball shows bank angle, not coordination, so she should level the wings with aileron and leave both rudder pedals alone until the ball centers
questions.why: In the climb, torque and P-factor roll and yaw the airplane left, so the pilot holds right rudder and aileron pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. The AFH says the design compensates for P-factor and propeller slipstream in powered flight; in a glide those effects disappear but the compensation remains, so slight left rudder pressure is likely needed, and the controls need bigger deflections because of the slow airflow [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. The PHAK adds that built-in compensation is set for cruise speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. 'Likely' is the AFH's word: confirm what your trainer needs before you teach it.
